Article Title: First puffin chick in 30 years just emerged from England's south coast after 15 weeks of careful monitoring, giving new hope to the country's last mainland colony
Article Text:
Why this puffin chick is such a big conservation success

How conservationists confirmed the chick's survival

Where is Dancing Ledge?



From more than 40 pairs to just three

Why researchers stayed away from the nest



Are puffins under threat?

What this means for the future of the colony

A tiny puffin chick has achieved something conservationists on England's south coast had not witnessed in three decades. After 15 weeks of careful monitoring by National Trust volunteers and seabird expert Dr Richard Caldow, the chick was photographed emerging from a rocky crevice at Dancing Ledge on Dorset's Isle of Purbeck. The sighting marks the first confirmed puffin chick at England's last remaining mainland south coast colony in around 30 years. With the colony now reduced to just three breeding pairs from more than 40 in the 1950s, the successful fledging has been hailed as a rare conservation milestone and a welcome sign that the fragile population still has a chance to recover.The newly spotted puffling represents far more than an adorable wildlife moment. It is the first confirmed breeding success at the Dorset colony in around 30 years, ending decades of uncertainty over whether the birds could still reproduce successfully on England's south coast.Atlantic puffins are among Britain's best-loved seabirds, but breeding colonies have declined in several parts of their range due to changing marine conditions, food shortages and other environmental pressures. With only three breeding pairs left at Dancing Ledge, every successful chick is considered vital for the colony's future.The breeding season was monitored for 15 weeks by National Trust volunteers alongside seabird specialist Dr Richard Caldow. Rather than approaching the nest, the team relied on trail cameras and long-distance observations to avoid disturbing the birds.One of the clearest signs that a chick was growing inside the burrow came when adult puffins were repeatedly seen carrying small fish back to the nesting crevice. The monitoring eventually paid off when cameras captured the puffling emerging from the cliffside burrow before later fledging successfully.Dancing Ledge is a dramatic limestone platform on the Isle of Purbeck in Dorset, forming part of the Jurassic Coast, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The rugged cliffs have long provided nesting habitat for seabirds, including puffins.Although the UK is home to hundreds of thousands of puffins across large island colonies in Scotland, Wales and northern England, the Purbeck birds are unique because they represent England's last remaining mainland colony on the south coast.The colony's decline has been dramatic. Historical records show that more than 40 breeding pairs nested around Dancing Ledge during the 1950s. Today, only three pairs remain.Scientists believe the decline is linked to several factors, including changing sea temperatures, reduced availability of small fish such as sand eels, and the challenges faced by a tiny, isolated population. Because so few birds remain, even a single successful breeding season is regarded as a major achievement.Puffins are highly sensitive during the breeding season and may abandon their nests if disturbed. To minimise the risk, conservationists kept the nesting location confidential and used remote cameras instead of direct inspections.The careful approach allowed researchers to observe natural behaviour without interfering with the adults as they fed and protected the chick. The successful fledging is being seen as evidence that low-impact monitoring can play an important role in conserving vulnerable seabird populations.Yes. The Atlantic puffin (Fratercula arctica) is classified as Vulnerable on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List because populations have declined across much of their range.The UK remains one of the species' global strongholds, with large colonies on islands such as the Farne Islands, Skomer, Bempton Cliffs, the Isle of May, Orkney and Shetland. However, mainland colonies are exceptionally rare, making the survival of the Dorset birds especially important.Conservationists have stressed that one chick does not mean the colony has recovered, but it does provide genuine reason for optimism. The successful breeding proves that the remaining puffins are still capable of raising young under the right conditions.The National Trust and its partners plan to continue monitoring the birds in future breeding seasons while protecting their nesting habitat from disturbance. If more chicks successfully fledge in the coming years, England's last mainland puffin colony could gradually begin rebuilding after decades of decline.
Article Summary: The chick was photographed emerging from a rocky crevice at Dancing Ledge on Dorset's Isle of Purbeck. The sighting marks the first confirmed puffin chick at England's last remaining mainland south coast colony in around 30 years. With the colony reduced to just three breeding pairs from more than 40 in the 1950s, the successful fledging has been hailed as a rare conservation milestone.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Dave Bautista: "I'm a poor kid from the streets. What I've been able to achieve has really just been through hard work and…" - an inspiring lesson on resilience, self-belief and tu
Article Text:
Dave Bautista (Image: Wikipedia)

Quote of the day by Dave Bautista

"I'm a poor kid from the streets. What I've been able to achieve has really just been through hard work and not letting anyone tell me that I couldn't do something. I always try to encourage people to just pursue your dreams"

What is the meaning behind Dave Bautista’s quote

Why where you start does not decide where you finish

The real story behind his career change

Why hard work stays essential even after talent gets you noticed

Why self-belief matters, especially when others doubt you

Why rejection rarely means the end of the road

Why pursuing a dream actually requires doing something

Other famous quotes by Dave Bautista

"I'm not afraid to go up to people and pick their brains and ask for advice. That's how you get better. That's how I've gotten better at everything I've ever done."

"I had been struggling to get roles in Hollywood for three and a half years after leaving the WWE. My agent turned me down three times before he even decided to take me on as a client."

"I was a poor kid. I came from nothing. We didn't have any money; a lot of times we didn't have any food. And now, all of a sudden, I'm a superhero in a Marvel movie. Talk about the American dream."

Why this still matters today

Success stories tend to look simple from the outside. People see the awards, the fame, the money, but rarely the years of struggle and rejection that came first. Dave Bautista , the actor and former professional wrestler, is open about exactly that gap. "I'm a poor kid from the streets," he said. "What I've been able to achieve has really just been through hard work and not letting anyone tell me that I couldn't do something. I always try to encourage people to just pursue your dreams." He is not hiding where he started. He is pointing straight at it, treating his own difficult beginning as part of the story rather than something to keep quiet about once success arrived.Bautista begins by naming his own background honestly, "a poor kid from the streets," rather than glossing over it. What follows explains what he believes actually made the difference between staying stuck and getting somewhere, hard work paired with a flat refusal to accept other people's doubts as his own limits. The quote ends on encouragement, telling people to actually pursue their dreams rather than simply hold them at arm's length.People are born into very different circumstances, some with real financial security, others with poverty and instability from the beginning.Those differences are genuinely real and genuinely hard. What Bautista's own life shows is that a difficult start does not automatically decide the ending. Circumstances shape the path. They do not always control the destination.Bautista's shift from wrestling into acting was far from instant. He has openly described struggling to get roles in Hollywood for three and a half years after leaving WWE. His own current agent, the one who eventually took him on, actually turned him down three times before finally agreeing to represent him. That is not a story of overnight success. It is a story of getting rejected repeatedly and simply not stopping.He has also connected his childhood directly to where that persistence eventually led. "I was a poor kid. I came from nothing," he has said. "We didn't have any money; a lot of times we didn't have any food. And now, all of a sudden, I'm a superhero in a Marvel movie." That gap, between a childhood without enough food and a career playing one of the most recognisable characters in a global film franchise, is really the whole story his quote is trying to compress into a single sentence.Talent can open a door. It rarely keeps that door open by itself. Every serious achievement takes sustained effort over a long stretch of time, learning new skills, absorbing setbacks, improving after failure, and staying disciplined even when nothing seems to be moving. Bautista credits his own success to persistence rather than luck or natural advantage, and his own career backs that up directly.Doubt shows up from all directions throughout life, sometimes from strangers, sometimes from people much closer. The real danger is letting that doubt quietly become your own belief about yourself. Self-belief here does not mean assuming success is guaranteed. It means trusting that improvement is possible through real effort, which is exactly the refusal Bautista describes as central to his own career, the decision to keep going regardless of who along the way told him he could not.Nearly everyone who eventually succeeds gets rejected somewhere along the way. Actors lose auditions. Athletes miss out on teams. Entrepreneurs hear investors say no. Bautista's own agent said no to him three separate times before saying yes. Rejection, in his story, became something to push through rather than a signal to stop.Dreams give people direction. Actual effort is what turns that direction into something real. Plenty of people have ambitions. Considerably fewer keep working toward them consistently once the early excitement fades. Bautista's quote is not encouraging wishful thinking. It is encouraging the harder, less glamorous version, developing skills, absorbing criticism, and continuing even when the goal still feels far away.Modern culture tends to highlight the finished result while skipping past the struggle that actually produced it. Bautista's honesty about his own background offers something different, an actual account of where he started and what it took to get somewhere else entirely. His message matters most for anyone who feels boxed in by their own circumstances. Poverty, rejection and doubt can all create real obstacles. None of them remove the possibility of what comes after, provided the effort behind it actually continues, day after day, long after it would have been easier to simply stop.
Article Summary: Dave Bautista is an actor and former professional wrestler. His quote of the day is: "I'm a poor kid from the streets. What I've been able to achieve has really just been through hard work and not letting anyone tell me that I couldn't do something" The quote ends on encouragement, telling people to pursue their dreams.

Article Title: In 1996, Indonesia's 'crazy' tree planter who was mocked for his mission planted 11,000 trees and turned barren hills into a green paradise
Article Text:
How deforestation triggered Wonogiri's drought and water crisis

How planting 11,000 banyan and ficus trees transformed Wonogiri's hills

Why many villagers opposed Sadiman's tree-planting mission

How thousands of trees helped revive Wonogiri's water supply

Why villagers now celebrate the man they once called crazy

When traversing the hills of Wonogiri in Central Java, today’s visitors might take the dense areas of greenery in stride. The springs nourish nearby villages, the farms have sufficient water for numerous harvests, and the slopes covered with trees conceal the bare ground that used to be visible before. However, very few would think of the fact that many changes took place thanks to the commitment of one man who dedicated many years to tree-planting efforts despite the lack of encouragement from the people around him.Now well-known as an environmentally conscious individual, Sadiman began his mission with a straightforward realisation. As a person who noticed the depletion of the local forest due to the constant farming and the disappearance of streams that provided water for many villages, he came up with his own way to fight that trend. His solution was not a governmental initiative or a large-scale project of some kind; it was decades of planting one tree after another and getting mocked by his neighbours who did not understand the sense of growing useless plants.The Wonogiri area has been known for many years to be dry. Rainfall is seasonal in nature, and the hilly nature of the area means that there is not much moisture retained after vegetation is destroyed in such areas.With the destruction of forests, cultivation and burning becoming common practices, the delicate balance that sustained the water supply of the area started dwindling away.People realised the negative impacts that had come about because of this. The rivers dried up, sources of water became inconsistent, and it became more difficult for people to carry out agricultural activities. In some cases, people could only farm during one cropping period because of lack of water.His attention settled on banyan and ficus trees, species known for their extensive root systems. Instead of growing only near villages or roads, he concentrated on higher ground where restoring vegetation could have a wider effect across surrounding catchment areas.As reported by Reuters in 2021, over more than two decades, he planted at least 11,000 trees across roughly 250 hectares (617 acres). The work progressed gradually. There was no sudden change to the landscape, only years of repeated planting and waiting for young trees to establish themselves.As the roots spread through the soil, they helped improve the ground's ability to absorb and retain rainfall. The thicker vegetation also reduced erosion on exposed slopes, allowing water to filter underground instead of running quickly downhill after storms.Many local residents questioned why anyone would spend so much effort planting banyan trees. Traditional beliefs surrounding the species meant some villagers associated them with spirits and avoided them altogether. Others simply saw little reason to exchange productive farmland or livestock for slow-growing trees whose benefits were far from immediate.Sadiman financed much of his work himself. Saplings became part of an unusual economy in which he traded or sold plants, including cloves and jackfruit, to support the continuing expansion of his nursery. At times he even exchanged livestock to obtain more young trees for planting.Some neighbours regarded these decisions as evidence that he had lost his judgement. The criticism continued for years, even as more hillsides slowly turned green.New springs were formed in areas which did not have any water source before, thus ensuring water source for the nearby community. The villages made use of pipes to get water directly into the households whereas the farmers got a more dependable water source for their agricultural purposes.For those families which were having a hard time due to lack of water, now they got water in a more convenient form. In addition, the farming was done two or three times a year as the source of water became more dependable.The trees kept on growing, thus perpetuating the process as they helped to conserve soil moisture.Public opinion changed only after visible results became impossible to ignore. People who had once questioned Sadiman's choices began pointing to the healthier hillsides and restored water sources as evidence of what sustained reforestation could achieve. Local residents who remembered the criticism now acknowledge that the project has benefited several villages by supporting reliable supplies of clean water.The transformation did not happen through rapid engineering or large financial investment. It emerged through patient ecological recovery, with each planting season adding another layer to a landscape that had spent years deteriorating.
Article Summary: The Wonogiri area of Central Java has been known for many years to be dry. deforestation triggered a drought and water crisis. Sadiman noticed the depletion of the local forest due to the constant farming and the disappearance of streams that provided water for many villages. His solution was not a governmental initiative or a large-scale project of some kind; it was decades of planting one tree after another.

Article Title: Bald eagle couple Jackie and Shadow's viral livestream raised $10 million to save their California forest home from luxury development
Article Text:
How Jackie and Shadow's viral livestream helped save their California forest home

Why the Moon Camp property was under threat

How the $10 million fundraising campaign came together

The donation that pushed the campaign over the finish line

What happens to Jackie and Shadow's habitat now?

A conservation effort decades in the making

Millions of people across the world have spent years watching bald eagle pair Jackie and Shadow build their nest, lay eggs, raise chicks and endure harsh winters through a 24/7 livestream in California's Big Bear Valley. What began as a simple wildlife camera has now become the driving force behind one of the biggest conservation victories in recent years. Inspired by the famous eagle couple, supporters rallied to raise $10 million to purchase and permanently protect a forested property that was set to become a luxury housing development. The campaign not only safeguarded the eagles' home but also demonstrated how online communities can turn admiration for wildlife into meaningful environmental action.Jackie and Shadow are among the world's most recognisable wild bald eagles thanks to a 24/7 nest camera operated by Friends of Big Bear Valley. Millions of viewers have followed the pair through multiple nesting seasons, watching everything from egg laying and hatching to snowstorms, feeding routines and the fledging of young eaglets. Their story has attracted a devoted global audience that extends far beyond birdwatchers.That emotional connection proved invaluable when conservationists warned that a nearby forest known as Moon Camp, an important feeding ground for the eagles, faced imminent development. Thousands of viewers who had spent years following Jackie and Shadow responded by donating to a fundraising campaign aimed at protecting the land. The remarkable public response transformed a beloved wildlife livestream into a real-world conservation movement.The campaign centred on Moon Camp, a 63-acre forested property on the north shore of Big Bear Lake near Fawnskin, California. Located less than a mile from Jackie and Shadow's nest, the area serves as one of the bald eagles' primary hunting grounds, providing access to fish and other prey essential for raising their young.A developer planned to convert the property into a luxury residential community featuring around 50 custom homes, a marina with boat slips and associated infrastructure. Environmental organisations warned that construction, increased traffic, artificial lighting and greater human activity would fragment the habitat and permanently alter one of Southern California's most ecologically valuable landscapes.Friends of Big Bear Valley partnered with the San Bernardino Mountains Land Trust to purchase the Moon Camp property before the development deadline. The organisations set an ambitious goal of raising $10 million, a figure that initially seemed difficult to achieve within the available timeframe.The campaign gained momentum as Jackie and Shadow's story spread through social media and news outlets. More than 25,000 people contributed donations, with public giving accounting for nearly half of the total amount raised. The fundraising goal was officially reached on July 24, 2026, days before the deadline, ensuring the property could be acquired for permanent conservation.A significant turning point came when Anna and Greg Brockman contributed more than $5.5 million, helping the campaign surpass its fundraising target. Their donation complemented thousands of smaller public contributions, illustrating how large philanthropic gifts and grassroots fundraising can work together to achieve ambitious conservation goals.According to Friends of Big Bear Valley, the funds will cover not only the purchase of the land but also closing costs, taxes, legal expenses and long-term stewardship. This ensures that the property will remain protected well into the future rather than facing renewed development pressures.With the fundraising campaign complete, the San Bernardino Mountains Land Trust will purchase Moon Camp and permanently preserve it as protected habitat. Instead of becoming an exclusive residential community, the land will continue to support bald eagles and many other native species that depend on the forest ecosystem.The preserved area is home to wildlife including San Bernardino flying squirrels, native birds and rare mountain plants. Conservationists say protecting the property also helps maintain ecological connectivity throughout Big Bear Valley, benefiting the broader ecosystem beyond Jackie and Shadow alone.Although the viral fundraising campaign unfolded in 2026, efforts to stop development at Moon Camp began more than two decades ago. Environmental groups had long argued that the proposed housing project threatened sensitive wildlife habitat and one of the region's most biodiverse landscapes.Jackie and Shadow's growing popularity gave those longstanding concerns an international audience. People who had never visited Big Bear Valley became emotionally invested in preserving the eagles' home after watching their daily lives unfold online. That unprecedented public engagement ultimately helped conservation groups secure the land before construction could begin.The success of the Moon Camp campaign illustrates how digital technology is reshaping wildlife conservation. Livestreams are often seen as educational tools, but Jackie and Shadow's story shows they can also mobilise global communities to protect vulnerable habitats.
Article Summary: Jackie and Shadow are among the world's most recognisable wild bald eagles thanks to a 24/7 nest camera operated by Friends of Big Bear Valley. Millions of viewers have followed the pair through multiple nesting seasons, watching everything from egg laying and hatching to snowstorms, feeding routines and the fledging of young eaglets. Conservationists warned that a nearby forest known as Moon Camp, an important feeding ground for the eagles, faced imminent development. Thousands of viewers who had spent years following Jackie and Shadow responded by donating to a fundraising campaign aimed at protecting the land.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Queen Elizabeth: "When life seems hard, the courageous do not lie down and accept defeat; instead, they…" - a timeless lesson on courage, perseverance and hope in difficult times
Article Text:
Queen Elizabeth

Quote of the day by Queen Elizabeth II

"When life seems hard, the courageous do not lie down and accept defeat; instead, they are all the more determined to struggle for a better future"

Exploring the true meaning of Queen Elizabeth’s quote

Why courage often shows up in small, everyday decisions

Why staying determined matters more than an immediate win

Why hope, in this quote, is something you actually do

How the Queen's own life reflected this idea

Why hardship can build genuine strength

How to actually use this idea day to day

Other memorable quotes by Queen Elizabeth

"Grief is the price we pay for love."

"It has always been easy to hate and destroy. To build and to cherish is much more difficult."

"We all need to get the balance right between action and reflection."

"It's worth remembering that it is often the small steps, not the giant leaps, that bring about the most lasting change."

What this quote means in today’s world

Everyone goes through periods when life feels genuinely hard, illness, money worries, loss, setbacks at work, moments when the future feels uncertain. The easy response is often to give up trying. Queen Elizabeth II offered a different way of thinking about those moments in her Christmas broadcast on the 25th of December 2008. "When life seems hard, the courageous do not lie down and accept defeat," she said. "Instead, they are all the more determined to struggle for a better future." She was not pretending life is easy. She was simply describing what she believed made the difference between giving up and pushing on, a distinction she had plenty of occasion to think about across seven decades on the throne.The quote starts honestly, with "when life seems hard." There is no pretence here that difficulty is rare or that everyone avoids it. Everyone runs into stretches where progress feels painfully slow and obstacles seem too big to get past, whatever their circumstances happen to be.What follows is the actual point. Courage does not mean feeling no fear or no pain. It means refusing to let those feelings decide what happens next.The quote ends by pointing forward, towards "a better future," suggesting that hardship, faced properly, can actually sharpen someone's resolve rather than weaken it.People tend to picture courage as something dramatic, a single big moment of bravery. More often, it looks much smaller than that. Getting up and going back to work after a real disappointment. Asking for help during a genuinely hard time. Supporting a family through money troubles. Starting again after a business or a career falls apart. Continuing treatment through a long illness. None of these moments make headlines, yet each one takes the same basic quality, choosing to keep going anyway.A setback can feel like the end of the road, a rejected job application, a failed exam, a lost job, a broken relationship. In reality, most of these moments turn out to be turning points rather than final endings. Staying determined does not guarantee instant success. It simply keeps the door open for a future success that giving up would close for good. Someone who keeps learning and adjusting after a setback still has options that someone who quits no longer does.Hope often gets treated as just wishing things will get better on their own. This quote describes something more active. The courageous are "determined to struggle" for a better future, meaning hope only really means something once effort gets attached to it. Simply waiting for circumstances to improve is a very different thing from actually taking steps, however small, towards making that improvement happen.Elizabeth became heir to the throne during the turmoil of the Second World War and went on to reign through decades of huge social and political change. Her time as monarch included economic crises, constitutional disputes, terrorist attacks and, near the end of her reign, the Covid-19 pandemic. Across many of her speeches, she returned again and again to the same themes, endurance, duty, and the belief that difficulties can be overcome through shared effort and persistence. This particular quote fits that pattern closely.Nobody goes looking for suffering, yet difficult experiences do tend to build qualities that easier times rarely produce. Patience grows when progress is slow. Resilience develops through actually recovering from setbacks. Empathy deepens once someone has been through real struggle themselves, since it becomes much easier to recognise the same struggle in someone else. None of this glorifies hardship for its own sake. It simply recognises that adversity, met with real determination, can end up becoming a source of genuine strength rather than something that only leaves damage behind.Focus on the very next step rather than trying to solve the whole problem at once. Keep up routines that support your health, work and relationships, especially when things are difficult. Ask for support from family, friends or professionals rather than struggling entirely alone. Treat setbacks as something to learn from rather than proof that you have failed. And keep the long view in mind, since most difficult periods, however overwhelming they feel at the time, do eventually pass, even when it is genuinely hard to believe that while you are still in the middle of one.What makes this quote last is the balance it strikes. It never pretends suffering is not real, and it never promises every struggle will end quickly or easily. It simply offers a way of thinking about hard times, that courage is measured by the decision to keep pushing toward something better, even while the present moment still feels genuinely difficult. That is really the whole message packed into one sentence, and it explains why people keep returning to these words years after she first said them, long after the specific Christmas broadcast that produced them has been largely forgotten.
Article Summary: "When life seems hard, the courageous do not lie down and accept defeat" Queen Elizabeth II said this in her Christmas broadcast on the 25th of December 2008. Courage does not mean feeling no fear or no pain. It means refusing to let those feelings decide what happens next.

Article Title: 10 killed, nearly 100 injured in Russian strike on Ukraine defence event
Article Text:
Addressing the nation, Zelenskyy blamed Russia for the attack.

At least 10 people were killed and nearly 100 injured after a Russian ballistic missile struck a defence industry event in Ukraine's Kyiv region on Friday, prompting President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to criticise the decision to hold such a gathering during wartime.Ukraine's Emergency Services said rescue operations at the site, located north of the capital, had been completed. Images released by the agency showed emergency workers searching through piles of rubble near several residential houses.Addressing the nation, Zelenskyy blamed Russia for the attack but also questioned the decision to organise a defence-related exhibition while the war continues."Of course, the cause of this attack is Russian missiles, nothing but Russian terror," he said, according to news agency Reuters."However, we have said a thousand times that under these wartime conditions, with such an enemy, it is absolutely unacceptable to hold any weapons exhibitions with large crowds of people, especially near residential buildings."The event, organised by a drone manufacturers' association, was being held a short distance from the outskirts of Kyiv. A spokesperson for Ukraine's General Staff said the venue did not fall under the military's jurisdiction, but stressed that any such event should have been conducted with "maximum security measures".Kyiv regional acting governor Ruslan Oliynyk announced that Saturday would be observed as a day of mourning following the strike.The Ukrainian Council of Defence Industry confirmed that representatives of the country's defence sector were present when the missile hit, but said it had not organised the event.Valerii Borovyk, founder of Ukrainian drone company First Contact, told local media that the missile struck a training ground where the exhibition was taking place.Ukraine's Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko said a criminal investigation had been launched to examine whether officials failed in their duties while organising and conducting the event.Russia also carried out attacks in several other parts of Ukraine on Friday. In the eastern city of Sloviansk, a Russian aerial bomb killed five people and injured nine, according to regional governor Vadym Filashkin. He later said another evening strike on the city injured 16 more people and damaged residential buildings.In the northern Sumy region, a Russian drone attack killed two people, regional governor Oleh Hryhorov said.Meanwhile, in the south-eastern city of Zaporizhzhia, a Russian strike set a shopping centre on fire and injured several people.Russia and Ukraine have repeatedly accused each other of targeting civilians since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, although both sides deny deliberately attacking civilian populations.
Article Summary: At least 10 people killed and nearly 100 injured after a Russian ballistic missile struck a defence industry event in Ukraine's Kyiv region on Friday. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia for the attack but also questioned the decision to organise a defence-related exhibition.

Article Title: 'I will come to fight': Netanyahu hits back at Mamdani over 'not welcome in New York City' remarks
Article Text: Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday hit back at New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani after the latter said he was "not welcome" in the city and backed the International Criminal Court's (ICC) arrest warrant against him. Declaring that he would travel to New York in September to address the United Nations General Assembly, Netanyahu accused the mayor of "fomenting hate" and dismissed the war-crimes allegations against him.Speaking to Fox News' Sunday Morning Futures, Netanyahu said, "My answer to Mamdani, I will come to New York to fight for the truth of the Jewish people.""I intend to come and speak the truth, speak for Israel and for the Israeli-American alliance from the podium of the United Nations," he added.Netanyahu's remarks came days after Mamdani said Israeli leaders facing ICC charges were not welcome in New York. The mayor also said that while New York City did not have the legal authority to execute the ICC's arrest warrant, he believed the US federal government should do so."Benjamin Netanyahu is not welcome in New York City, nor is any other war criminal at large. As I've said, I agree with the ICC that Benjamin Netanyahu should be arrested and tried for his crimes, as I do for anyone else charged by the ICC," Mamdani had said.He had also told media outlet, The New York Times, that his administration was engaged in an "active conversation" with the New York City law department to determine the city's legal authority if Netanyahu visits for the UN General Assembly in September.Responding to the criticism, Netanyahu accused Mamdani of siding with Hamas. "What Mamdani is supporting, his wife, his family - he celebrated October 7th massacre, the worst massacre against Jews since the Holocaust," Netanyahu said.He claimed the group had carried out killings, sexual violence and hostage-taking, concluding, "That's who he's supporting."Rejecting allegations of genocide against Israel, Netanyahu said, "They're the ones who are responsible for genocide." He added, "The genocide charge belongs to our enemies. What we're doing is trying to fight this genocidal terrorist organization... That's where the real criminals are."The Israeli prime minister also criticised Mamdani's leadership, saying previous New York mayors sought to unite the city. "Mamdani is aligning himself with the criminals... but the worst thing is that he's tormenting his own citizens, his own voters," Netanyahu said.He further alleged that the mayor was "fomenting hate", adding, "He's supposed to be the mayor of all New Yorkers: Jews, Christians, Muslims, everyone. But he's trying to turn one group against the other and he's foisting hate and fear."Netanyahu also linked Mamdani's remarks to a recent stabbing incident outside a New York synagogue, saying, "I don't think it's accidental that after he made this hate speech against Israel and against me, the next day a Jew is stabbed coming out of a synagogue... with a cry of 'Allahu Akbar'."A 51-year-old man, identified as Raul Morales, has been charged with two counts of attempted murder as hate crimes after allegedly attacking an Asian man and a Jewish man on Manhattan's Upper West Side on Thursday. Police said Morales shouted "Allahu Akbar" during both attacks. The Jewish victim had just left a synagogue.
Article Summary: Netanyahu says he will travel to New York in September to address the United Nations General Assembly. Mayor Zohran Mamdani had said Israeli leaders facing ICC charges were not welcome in New York. Netanyahu accused the mayor of "fomenting hate"

Article Title: A rural Chile community struggling with drought restored its water supply by protecting a watershed, planting native trees and rebuilding the soil that holds rain
Article Text:

A rainy island faced shortages

Restoring nature

A small rural community on Chile's Chiloe Island has ended years of dependence on emergency water tanker trucks by restoring its forests, protecting its watershed and building a community-managed water system.The project took years of planning and work by local residents, researchers and landowners. Rather than only building pipes and storage tanks, the community focused on improving the health of the land that supplies water. Nearly seven years after the system began operating, residents continue to receive a reliable water supply.The experience has now been turned into a practical guide for other rural communities that are facing water shortages.While the exact model cannot be copied everywhere, the approach of protecting the water source before building infrastructure can be adapted to many places. The information was published by Chile's Institute of Ecology and Biodiversity.Chiloe Island is known for heavy rainfall. The Ancud area receives around 87 inches of rain in an average year. Even so, the Catruman community experienced serious water shortages.The problem was not the total amount of rainfall but when it fell. Most rain comes during winter, while summer rainfall has reduced over the years. During the dry season, small streams can stop flowing for as long as four months.As a result, many families struggled to get enough water. Before the project started, 64% of households depended partly on water supplied by tanker trucks. Around 37% relied completely on tanker deliveries for six months or more.Municipal records from the 2014-2015 drought show that tanker deliveries provided an average of only 2.4 gallons of water per person each day. That limited amount had to cover drinking, cooking, washing, caring for animals and watering vegetable gardens.To solve the problem, the community decided to improve the entire watershed. A watershed is the area of land where rainwater collects and flows into streams, rivers or springs. Keeping the land healthy helps water soak into the ground and flow steadily throughout the year.Residents worked with researchers to map Catruman's 36 microcatchments, small areas that collect rainwater. They identified a stream that flowed throughout the year and partnered with upstream landowners to protect it.The team planted more than 500 native trees around damaged land and an old spring. These included ulmo, coihue, canelo, luma and arrayan trees, all native to southern Chile.They also dug small infiltration trenches on slopes. These shallow channels slow down rainwater allowing more of it to soak into the soil instead of flowing away. This helps recharge groundwater and keeps streams flowing longer during dry periods.After protecting the water source, the community built a gravity-fed water supply system. Water is collected at an intake point, passes through filters and is stored in a tank with a capacity of about 6,600 gallons. From there, it flows downhill through pipes to homes using gravity, eliminating the need for electric pumps.Because the system uses gravity, it reduces electricity costs and ongoing maintenance, making it more suitable for a small rural community.Even during the lowest measured summer flows, the stream supplied around 6.3 gallons of water every minute, or about 9,100 gallons each day.The estimated daily demand for 14 families and the local civic centre was about 2,640 gallons. This meant enough water remained in the stream to support the surrounding ecosystem.The project also focused on keeping the water clean. A constructed wetland was built near a home and a small cheese-making operation located upstream from the community's water intake.Constructed wetlands use plants and naturally occurring microorganisms to clean household wastewater. After treatment, the water can either be reused for irrigation or allowed to soak safely into the ground instead of flowing back into the community's water source.The project showed that increasing the amount of available water is only part of the challenge. Protecting water quality is equally important because pollution from wastewater, livestock or household activities can make a water source unsafe.Community members carried out much of the construction through traditional collective work gatherings known as 'mingas'.Residents also received training to maintain the pipes, filters and restoration areas. They formed a local organisation to collect fees, organise repairs and work with government agencies and landowners when needed.Community leader Galicia Mansilla said the changes had made a significant difference. "Before, we lived with a lot of uncertainty. Today, we have a system that works," Ecoticias reported.
Article Summary: Rural community on Chile's Chiloé Island restores its water supply. Project took years of planning and work by local residents, researchers and landowners. Rather than only building pipes and storage tanks, the community focused on improving the health of the land that supplies water. The experience has now been turned into a practical guide for other rural communities that are facing water shortages.

Article Title: 'Indian students made us all proud': Greta Thunberg joins London protest in solidarity

Greta Thunberg stands in solidarity with CJP-led student protest (Image: X@/epppyyy)
