Article Title: Donald Trump returns to White House Correspondents' dinner months after shooting forced postponement
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump attends the White House Correspondents' Association Dinner

US President Donald Trump on Friday attended the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) dinner, nearly three months after the annual event was postponed following a shooting outside the original venue.The US president is set to address journalists from major news organisations after months of clashes with the media over coverage and press access.Ahead of the event, White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said Trump's remarks would be "a combination of unifying yet vicious, and serious yet hilarious, all at the same time."The annual black-tie dinner, which celebrates press freedom and raises money for journalism scholarships, was postponed from April after a gunman attempted to breach a security checkpoint and opened fire outside the venue room at Washington Hilton, where Trump and members of his Cabinet were present.Friday's event is now being held at the Waldorf Astoria hotel under heightened security.Meanwhile, the suspect in the shooting, Cole Allen, later pleaded not guilty to charges including attempting to assassinate the president.The White House Correspondents' Association said the programme would include recognition of Secret Service officer Victor Gonzales, who was wounded while stopping the attacker, as well as Washington Hilton staff who assisted guests during the incident.Trump's appearance comes amid continued criticism from press freedom advocates over his administration's lawsuits against media organisations, restrictions on some journalists' access and other actions affecting the press. The White House has defended those measures, saying they are intended to improve accountability, protect sensitive information and address media bias.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump attended the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) dinner. The annual black-tie dinner was postponed from April after a gunman attempted to breach a security checkpoint and opened fire outside the venue room at Washington Hilton. The event is now being held at the Waldorf Astoria hotel under heightened security.

Article Title: Who is Karyna Shuliak, the woman Epstein left a diamond ring 'in contemplation of marriage'?
Article Text:
Karyna Shuliak, the woman identified as Jeffrey Epstein's longtime girlfriend (Image: X@/infodexx)

Karyna Shuliak, the woman identified as Jeffrey Epstein 's longtime girlfriend, has come under renewed public attention following the release of millions of pages of investigative files that shed light on their nearly eight-year relationship.Shuliak was the last person Epstein called before he died by suicide in a New York jail cell in August 2019.She met Epstein in 2011 after moving from Belarus to New York on a student visa. The documents show that the two developed a close relationship, with Epstein referring to her as his "favorite", providing financial support, and helping her pursue her goal of becoming a dentist, as cited by The New York Times.The records also indicate that he transferred nearly $1 million to her over the years and sent money to her parents in Belarus.Epstein had reportedly assisted Shuliak in gaining admission to Columbia University's dental school after an initial rejection and later paid for her tuition. They also describe how he arranged a same-sex marriage between Shuliak and one of his assistants, which would enable her to acquire a green card.A congressional report later questioned whether the marriage was "illusory", though immigration authorities have not challenged her citizenship.Federal prosecutors' emails show that Epstein bought Broadway tickets for The Lion King for Shuliak and her roommate, took them out to restaurants, and arranged a helicopter tour of Manhattan. By July 2011, Shuliak had visited Epstein's New Mexico ranch and, months later, his private island in the US Virgin Islands.Shortly before his death in 2019, Epstein amended his will to leave Shuliak a substantial share of his then-estimated $600 million fortune, including a large diamond ring described in a handwritten note as being "in contemplation of marriage".The exact amount she is expected to inherit remains unclear, as estate records show its value has since fallen to between $120 million and $200 million after payouts to victims, with dozens of beneficiaries, including his brother Mark Epstein's children, also named in the will.Despite the prospect of a sizeable inheritance, Shuliak continued pursuing a career in dentistry. In 2023, she returned to New York to enrol in a postdoctoral dental programme at Columbia University, a requirement for obtaining a licence to practise in the state.According to admissions records reviewed by The New York Times, the same two dentists who had supported her admission in 2012 again assisted her, with Dr James Fine creating a special faculty internship for her at the Midtown Manhattan practice he shared with Dr Thomas Magnani.
Article Summary: Karyna Shuliak met Jeffrey Epstein in 2011 after moving from Belarus to New York on a student visa. She was the last person Epstein called before he died by suicide in a New York jail cell in August 2019. Documents show that the two developed a close relationship, with Epstein referring to her as his "favorite" and providing financial support.

Article Title: Two killed, five wounded in Seattle mass shooting at food festival
Article Text:
Representative image (AP)

A mass shooting at Seattle Center on Sunday evening left two people dead and at least five others injured, authorities told Seattle Times.The shooting took place around 6 pm local time at Seattle Center, where thousands of people had gathered for the annual Bite of Seattle food festival.Witnesses reported hearing a barrage of gunshots before panic spread across the venue. People were seen running in different directions and taking cover as the gunfire erupted across the 74-acre park complex.Police and emergency responders rushed to the scene, while authorities launched an investigation into the shooting.A witness told local media, "I heard bang, bang, bang, and then people started screaming."A Seattle Police department spokesperson said he was on his way to the scene and could not provide more details.Kayla Carris, 22, who was sitting outside the Armory during the Bite of Seattle festival, said panic spread quickly after the shooting."People suddenly started screaming and running inside the Seattle Center Armory building," she said. "Everyone was dropping their things and running. Everyone."
Article Summary: Shooting took place around 6 pm local time at Seattle Center, where thousands of people had gathered for the annual Bite of Seattle food festival. People were seen running in different directions and taking cover as the gunfire erupted across the 74-acre park complex. Authorities launched an investigation into the shooting.

Article Title: Indian-origin US lawmakers vow to fight anti-India hate, urge diaspora to join politics
Article Text:
Indian-origin US Congressmen Shri Thanedar. (AP Photo)

'We are here to stay'

Indian-origin US Congressmen Shri Thanedar and Raja Krishnamoorthi vowed to push back against anti-India and anti-immigrant hatred in the United States, urging Indian-Americans to play a bigger role in public life by contesting elections at all levels.The Democratic lawmakers made the remarks during an event in Washington marking the 250th anniversary of US Independence, organised by the Indian American Committee.Both said the Indian-American community has become an integral part of American society and should be more strongly represented in politics.Thanedar, who represents Michigan, said the US has always been a nation of immigrants and warned against growing hostility towards immigrant communities."The hate that we have seen across America against immigrants must not be tolerated,” Thanedar was quoted as saying by news agency PTI.“We must demand that immigrants, their culture and their contribution to this great country be honoured and respected every day," he said.Calling for greater political participation, Thanedar said the community could bring about change only by entering public service."We need to see more Indian Americans in our political arena serving at various levels — local, state and national," he said.Krishnamoorthi, the Illinois Congressman, said Indian-Americans would continue to stand up against anti-India and anti-Hindu hatred.Recalling an incident in which he faced calls to be deported to India, he declared, "We are here to stay. We are part of the fabric of this country. And on America's 250th birthday, we are going to fight back."He added that the fight would extend beyond anti-India sentiment."We're going to fight back against anti-Indian hatred. We're going to fight back against anti-Hindu hatred. We're going to fight back against all forms of prejudice, bigotry and discrimination toward anybody," he said.Krishnamoorthi, who lost the Democratic primary for the US Senate from Illinois earlier this year, said Indian-Americans are among the country's best-educated and most prosperous communities.He noted that they make up around 10 per cent of US doctors and own about 60 per cent of hotels and motels in the country.He urged members of the diaspora to contest elections for city councils, state legislatures, the US House of Representatives and the Senate, irrespective of party affiliation."I don't care if you're a Republican, independent or Democrat. It's time to run because the stakes could not be higher. We are being tested," he said.Krishnamoorthi's remarks come days after he warned of what he described as a rise in anti-India hate incidents in the US.In a post on X earlier this week, he cited an incident in Frisco, Texas, where a group of alleged white supremacists gathered outside City Hall, displayed anti-India messages and tore an Indian flag.According to the Congressman, the group shouted slogans including "Go back to India" and "Stop the Hindu takeover of Texas."Calling for unity against hate, Krishnamoorthi said discrimination should be opposed regardless of who is targeted.His comments came amid wider concerns over racism, anti-immigrant rhetoric and hate targeting minority communities in the United States.
Article Summary: Indian-origin US Congressmen Shri Thanedar and Raja Krishnamoorthi vowed to push back against anti-India and anti-immigrant hatred in the United States. The Democratic lawmakers made the remarks during an event in Washington marking the 250th anniversary of US Independence.

Article Title: California stabbing: Five injured after drunken altercation; 18-year-old arrested
Article Text:
California stabbing leaves five injured

Five men were injured in a stabbing following an alleged drunken altercation in Old Sacramento, California, early Saturday, and an 18-year-old suspect has been arrested, police said.According to the New York Post, the violence allegedly began as a booze-fueled argument that escalated into a stabbing near Front Street and K Street shortly after 3 am.Police found three men with stab wounds at the scene, while two more victims later arrived at a local hospital with injuries linked to the same incident.All five victims were hospitalised and were in stable condition as of Saturday afternoon, authorities said.Police arrested 18-year-old Sacramento resident Ezekiel Griffis after identifying him as a person of interest in the investigation. He was booked into the Sacramento County Main Jail on assault charges.Three people were initially detained following the incident, but two were later released. Police said the investigation remains ongoing.The stabbing has renewed attention on safety concerns in Old Sacramento, which has witnessed several high-profile violent incidents in recent years.In 2021, the district saw a large brawl involving around 50 juveniles and a homicide later that summer, prompting calls from residents and business owners for stricter action against street partying, public intoxication and other disturbances.
Article Summary: Five men were injured in a stabbing in Old Sacramento, California, early Saturday. Police found three men with stab wounds at the scene, while two more victims later arrived at a local hospital with injuries linked to the same incident. Police arrested 18-year-old Sacramento resident Ezekiel Griffis after identifying him as a person of interest.

Article Title: FBI's 'most wanted' suspect in $32 million Covid fraud arrested in Jamaica: Kash Patel
Article Text:
Elaine Angene Escoe

Allegedly used fake identity in Jamaica

Kash Patel hails latest FBI arrest

Other defendants already convicted

A woman on the FBI's Most Wanted Fraudsters list has been extradited from Jamaica to the United States after allegedly spending months on the run under a fake identity, FBI Director Kash Patel said.According to the US Department of Justice, Elaine Angene Escoe, 41, arrived in South Florida on Thursday after Jamaican authorities arrested her following a federal manhunt.Prosecutors allege she helped orchestrate a scheme that fraudulently obtained more than $32 million in taxpayer-funded Covid-19 relief funds before fleeing the US after failing to appear in federal court.Escoe was indicted in 2025 on charges including conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and multiple counts of money laundering.According to the US Department of Justice, Escoe fled to Jamaica after a federal arrest warrant was issued in May 2025.Authorities say she lived under the alias "Harley Newman" before investigators tracked her down with the help of a tip received by the FBI.The alleged fraud involved applications for multiple pandemic-era federal relief programs, including the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP), Restaurant Revitalization Fund (RRF), Shuttered Venue Operators Grant (SVOG) and Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL) program.Investigators allege Escoe and her co-conspirators submitted fraudulent applications supported by fake tax returns, fabricated bank records and other falsified financial documents to obtain relief funds.Some applications were allegedly filed for third parties in exchange for kickbacks of up to 50 per cent of the loan proceeds.Announcing the arrest, FBI Director Kash Patel said Escoe is the fourth alleged "Most Wanted Fraudster" captured in the past five weeks."Elaine Angene Escoe, on the run since May 2025, was captured in Jamaica while living under a fake identity of 'Harley Newman' and returned to the United States today to face justice," Patel said.He added that the FBI has brought back more than 30 high-value fugitives to the US since June and said the four fraud suspects arrested over the past five weeks are collectively accused of nearly $1.8 billion in fraud after spending more than 3,500 days on the run across three continents.The Justice Department said Escoe is the last remaining defendant charged in the alleged scheme.Five co-defendants have already been convicted or pleaded guilty. Alfred Davis received a 235-month prison sentence, while others were sentenced to terms ranging from 42 to 87 months.Escoe is expected to face federal proceedings in the Southern District of Florida. Authorities said her return was coordinated by the FBI, US Marshals Service, Homeland Security Investigations, the US State Department and Jamaican law enforcement agencies.
Article Summary: Elaine Angene Escoe, 41, arrived in South Florida on Thursday after Jamaican authorities arrested her following a federal manhunt. Prosecutors allege she helped orchestrate a scheme that fraudulently obtained more than $32 million in taxpayer-funded Covid-19 relief funds. Escoe was indicted in 2025 on charges including conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud and money laundering.

Article Title: In 1958, Hawaii introduced barn owls to control rats in sugarcane fields; the owls spread across the islands and began killing endangered seabirds
Article Text:
In 1958, Hawaii introduced barn owls to control rats in sugarcane fields; the owls spread across the islands and began killing endangered seabirds. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

An owl released to protect the sugar industry

From rats to endangered seabirds

Newell’s Shearwaters and Hawaiian Petrels being hunted down by Barn owls. Now these two species listed under the US Endangered Species Act. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons.

A biological-control plan with an unexpected target

In the late 1950s, Hawaii brought in a predator to fight a pest. Barn owls were introduced to the islands as a biological-control measure against rats, which were considered a serious threat to the sugar industry. The plan appeared straightforward: release a natural hunter and allow it to reduce the rodent population.But the owls did not remain focused on rats. They established breeding populations, spread across the Hawaiian Islands and began hunting native seabirds. Some of their victims included endangered species whose populations were already under pressure from introduced predators, habitat loss and other threats.A study published in Marine Ornithology documented 379 cases of barn owl predation involving eight seabird species in Hawaii between 2011 and 2018. The victims included Newell’s Shearwaters and Hawaiian Petrels, both protected under the US Endangered Species Act. More recent research using DNA analysis has suggested that conventional monitoring may underestimate how frequently the owls prey on seabirds.According to the above research, barn owls (Tyto alba) were introduced to Hawaii in the late 1950s by the Hawaii Department of Agriculture as a biological control for rats, which were seen as a threat to sugarcane production.The initial introductions were done on Kauai, Oahu and Hawaii islands; and after that on Molokai. The idea was simple: instead of relying entirely on chemicals to control pests, introduce their natural predators.Barn Owls appeared to be a logical choice. They are skilled nocturnal hunters and commonly prey on rodents. But island ecosystems can be particularly vulnerable to introduced predators. Native species that evolved in isolation may have little experience with newly arrived hunters, while predators introduced for one purpose can encounter prey that was never part of the original plan. The owls also proved capable of moving beyond the areas where they had been released.Later research showed that the problem was not limited to isolated incidents. A study published in Marine Ornithology also notes that researchers from the Kaua‘i Endangered Seabird Recovery Project examined records collected during seabird monitoring on Kaua‘i and the nearby islets of Lehua and Moku‘ae‘ae. Between January 2011 and October 2018, they recorded 379 cases of Barn Owl predation involving eight seabird species. The most frequently recorded victims were Wedge-tailed Shearwaters, Black Noddies and Bulwer’s Petrels.But the records also included Newell’s Shearwaters and Hawaiian Petrels, two species listed under the US Endangered Species Act. Most of the birds were adults, which matters because the loss of breeding adults can have serious consequences for vulnerable populations. The researchers observed Barn Owls hunting adult seabirds in flight, entering burrows and killing birds near nesting sites. The owls also appeared capable of targeting areas where seabirds gathered. On Lehua Islet, researchers found numerous dead Black Noddies in an area near a sea cave where the birds bred. On another islet, 21 adult Bulwer’s Petrels were found dead during one survey.In a more recent study published in the Journal of Heredity , researchers used DNA metabarcoding to analyse swab samples from 55 Barn Owls captured on Kauai and Lehua. They detected DNA from six seabird taxa, including the endangered Hawaiian Petrel and Newell’s Shearwater. DNA from the two endangered species was found in 12 swabs from 11 owls. By comparison, conventional examination of stomach contents detected seabird remains in only one owl. The researchers said the results suggest that traditional methods may underestimate how often barn owls prey on seabirds.The Hawaii case shows that a predator introduced for one purpose may not remain focused on its intended pest or habitat. Introduced predators can also interact with local wildlife in ways that were not anticipated at the outset. The problem is especially acute on islands, where many seabirds nest in burrows or on small islets and may have few defences against an introduced aerial predator. Barn Owls can also move between islands and breeding areas, making it difficult to protect individual colonies by controlling owls in only one location.Another complication involves the relationship between rats and Barn Owls. Removing rats can benefit seabirds by reducing predation on their eggs and chicks. However, if rats form part of the owls' available prey, their removal could also alter the food available to Barn Owls and potentially affect what other prey they target. This makes predator management particularly complex in island ecosystems, where efforts to control one introduced species can influence the behaviour and ecological effects of another.
Article Summary: In 1958, Hawaii introduced barn owls to control rats in sugarcane fields. The owls spread across the islands and began killing endangered seabirds. Victims included Newell’s Shearwaters and Hawaiian Petrels, both protected under the US Endangered Species Act.

Article Title: In 1851, New York released house sparrows to eat caterpillars damaging city trees; within 50 years, the birds had colonised nearly the entire continental US
Article Text:
In 1851, New York released house sparrows to eat caterpillars damaging city trees; within 50 years, the birds had colonised nearly the entire continental US. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons.

A bird brought in to control pests

From Brooklyn to the Rocky Mountains

The release of a few sparrows in Brooklyn in 1851 was intended to combat the destruction of trees by insects. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

A successful introduction creates new problems

In 1851, a small group of birds was released in Brooklyn to eat insect pests and protect the city's trees. The house sparrow, a familiar bird across Europe and Asia, was introduced to New York in the 1850s as part of efforts to establish European birds in North America, with some supporters also viewing the species as potentially useful for controlling insect pests.According to American Bird Conservancy , within decades, the experiment had produced something far larger than its organisers had intended. The birds spread rapidly across the United States, adapting to cities, farms and human-built structures. By 1900, they had reached the Rocky Mountains, and additional introductions helped them establish populations across the West. In less than half a century, a bird that had not previously been present in North America had become a permanent part of the continent's urban landscape.The house sparrow (Passer domesticus) was introduced to Brooklyn in 1851 as part of an effort to control caterpillars and protect city trees from insect damage. However, the exact details of the first introduction have been debated.According to a study published in Biological Invasions , the historical record was re-examined and concluded that the first successful New York introduction may have involved just 16 birds, rather than the much larger numbers often reported in earlier accounts.The researchers argued that this small founding population may have been enough to establish the species in the city. It is a worrisome condition for conservationists when the population of a species drops to a few dozen. However, these house sparrows demonstrated something opposite and phenomenal. A small population of sparrows exploded into millions with favorable environmental conditions. Establishment of a new population by a small number of individual species is called the ‘founder effect.’ The founder effect is now being extensively explored in the fields of genetics, ecology, and conservation biology. It is quite interesting to study and draw reasoning because in the founder effect, only a small part of the original founding species’ genetic diversity is passed on to the new population. It means the newly established population can show significant differences in the genetic makeup from the original ‘founders.’ These descendants may develop distinct genetic characteristics over a long time. In this case, this tiny population of sparrows had an outsized impact on the local ecology. Its arrival reflected a broader 19th-century enthusiasm for introducing familiar European species to North America. Some releases were motivated by nostalgia, while others were intended to provide practical benefits such as pest control.The house sparrow appeared to offer both. It was small, adaptable and capable of feeding on insects. But its diet was broader than the caterpillars it had been brought in to control. House sparrows also eat seeds, grains and other food, allowing them to survive in a wide range of environments.The house sparrow's expansion did not stop in North America. Human introductions helped the species establish populations across much of the world, making it one of the most widely distributed birds on Earth. The bird also showed signs of geographical variation as its populations spread. Studies of North American house sparrows documented differences in traits such as body size and plumage between populations, showing that the species was not entirely uniform across its expanded range.In 1900, it had already spread to the Rocky Mountains. Additional introductions in the early 1870s in San Francisco and Salt Lake City helped the bird spread more quickly across the western United States. Today, the sparrow is widespread throughout North America except for Alaska and the far north of Canada. Its spread was not due to its reproductive ability alone. This sparrow was highly adaptable to landscapes modified by humans. It could nest in buildings, eaves, streetlights and other artificial nesting sites that few other birds use.The house sparrow's rapid expansion eventually turned it from a pest-control experiment into a species-management problem. The species is highly competitive around nesting sites and can displace native birds from nest boxes and other suitable cavities. The American Bird Conservancy notes that house sparrows can drive native species such as Eastern Bluebirds away from nest boxes and, in some cases, kill them while competing for nesting space.The bird's role in insect control was more complicated than its original supporters had expected. A 19th-century account published in Nature described the widespread belief that house sparrows would protect trees from caterpillars, while questioning how effectively they actually performed that role. The article also reported concerns that the introduced birds were displacing native species.The story of the house sparrow illustrates how introduced species can have difficult-to-control ecological effects. The release of a few sparrows in Brooklyn in 1851 was intended to combat the destruction of trees by insects. Instead, the species was able to colonise an entire continent and adapt to a human environment to become one of the most widespread birds in the world. In doing so, the experiment highlighted the species' adaptability and the potential impact introduced species can have.
Article Summary: The house sparrow (Passer domesticus) was introduced to Brooklyn in 1851 as part of an effort to control caterpillars and protect city trees. The birds spread rapidly across the United States, adapting to cities, farms and human-built structures. By 1900, they had reached the Rocky Mountains, and additional introductions helped them establish populations across the West. Today, the sparrow is widespread throughout North America except for Alaska and the far north of Canada.

Article Title: In 1929, Hawaii introduced Japanese white-eyes to control insects; they became its most abundant land bird and began competing with native birds for food
Article Text:
A courting pair of Japanese White-eyes (Zosterops japonicus) - Kauai, Hawaii. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

A bird brought in to fight insect pests

The competition was over food

In 1929, Hawaii introduced a small bird from Japan to help control insect pests. The Japanese white-eye, also known as the mejiro. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

When a biological-control measure becomes part of the problem

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you believe is the biggest threat to native Hawaiian bird species? Habitat loss Diseases 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

In 1929, Hawaii introduced a small bird from Japan to help control insect pests. The Japanese white-eye, also known as the mejiro, was brought to the islands because officials hoped it would feed on insects harmful to agriculture. Instead, the bird spread rapidly, established itself across the archipelago and became one of Hawaii's most abundant land birds.Its success, however, created a new ecological concern. As Japanese white-eyes became widespread, they began using many of the same food resources as native Hawaiian birds. Research later suggested that this competition placed additional pressure on native species already threatened by habitat loss, introduced predators and disease.According to a study published by Yale University , Japanese white-eye (Zosterops japonicus) was introduced into Oahu in 1929 through the efforts of Hawaii's Board of Commissioners of Agriculture and Forestry with the intention of using the bird to control insect pests as a biological agent. The bird proved to be highly adaptable to its surroundings. Japanese white-eyes feed on insects, fruits and nectar and have adapted to a variety of habitats including forest and agricultural environments.Once established, the birds spread across the islands. Their ability to exploit different food sources and habitats helped them become one of the most common birds in the Hawaiian Islands. It fed on fruit and helped disperse seeds, becoming deeply integrated into the islands' ecosystems.The concern was not that Japanese white-eyes attacked native birds directly. Instead, they could compete with them by exploiting similar food sources and feeding in the same parts of plants. Research published in Ecological Monographs found evidence of negative associations between Japanese white-eyes and several native Hawaiian forest birds. The researchers reported patterns consistent with competition involving species such as the ‘I‘iwi and ‘Elepaio, although they also noted that the effects varied between species and locations.A later study published in Current Biology provided further evidence of the pressure created by the introduced bird. Researchers examined Japanese white-eyes and eight native Hawaiian passerines and found substantial overlap in the resources and locations used for foraging. They also found that, after 2000, juveniles of every native species examined had lower body mass in areas where white-eye abundance had increased. Many also had shorter bills and tarsi, while smaller body size was associated with reduced survival in several species. During the same period, the endangered Hawai‘i ‘Akepa population was judged to have become non-viable. The findings suggested that competition did not have to involve direct aggression. When two species rely on similar resources, an abundant introduced species can gain an advantage simply by consuming or occupying the same resources as native birds.The Japanese white-eye's success in Hawaii illustrates how an introduced species can become part of an ecosystem in ways that extend beyond its original purpose. The birds compete with some native species for food, while their fruit-eating habits also allow them to disperse seeds as they move between plants. The species' history also highlights one of the challenges associated with biological control. Once an introduced animal establishes a breeding population, it can spread and interact with native species in ways that may not have been anticipated.The white-eye's presence is not the sole explanation for the pressures facing Hawaii's native birds, which are affected by several environmental threats. But its spread shows how an introduction intended to serve one purpose can have wider ecological consequences.
Article Summary: The Japanese white-eye (Zosterops japonicus) was introduced into Oahu in 1929 through the efforts of Hawaii's Board of Commissioners of Agriculture and Forestry with the intention of using the bird to control insect pests as a biological agent. The bird proved to be highly adaptable to its surroundings and have adapted to a variety of habitats including forest and agricultural environments. Their ability to exploit different food sources helped them become one of the most common birds in the Hawaiian Islands.

Article Title: Los Angeles coated more than 700,000 sq ft of dark asphalt with reflective material, and during a heatwave, parts of Pacoima saw air temperatures up to 1.9°C lower
Article Text:
Los Angeles coated 700,000 sq ft of dark asphalt with reflective material; during extreme heat, local air was up to 1.9°C cooler. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

A neighbourhood-scale test of reflective pavement

Cooler air does not mean every surface feels cooler

As global temperatures rise, the question may be less about one technology cooling an entire city and more about whether enough small-scale changes can make hot neighbourhoods safer during heat waves. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

A tool for hot cities, but not a standalone answer

Poll Vote & Share your view In your opinion, which factor most affects thermal comfort during extreme heat? Air temperature Surface temperature Humidity 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

In one of Los Angeles's hottest neighbourhoods, more than 700,000 square feet of dark asphalt was covered with a solar-reflective coating. The aim was simple: reduce the amount of heat absorbed by streets, car parks, playgrounds and other paved surfaces. According to research published in Environmental Research Communications , the experiment took place in Pacoima, a neighbourhood in the San Fernando Valley where summer heat can be intense. After the coating was applied, researchers found that the treated area was cooler than a nearby comparison area. During a September 2022 heatwave, afternoon air temperatures in some street segments of the treated area were up to 3.5°F (1.9°C) lower than in the comparison area.The result offered evidence that changing the surface of a city can influence the heat experienced around it. But the experiment also highlighted the limits of reflective pavement: cooling the air does not necessarily mean every aspect of outdoor heat exposure becomes more comfortable.The experiment was done in Pacoima in collaboration between Climate Resolve, a non-profit organisation, and GAF, a company that provided the reflective coating material.The coating was applied in over 700,000 square feet of dark asphalt. It included parts of roads, parking lots, basketball courts, and playgrounds. Dark asphalt absorbs a substantial part of the sun's rays and radiates it in the form of heat. Reflective pavements, on the other hand, reflect more sunlight instead of absorbing it. Scientists observed both areas and compared them to a neighbouring community with the same conditions but without the coating. The observation period was much longer than a single temperature reading.The study published in Environmental Research Communications also notes that the results varied according to weather conditions. On ordinary sunny days, the cooling effect on air temperatures was smaller. During an extreme heat event, however, the difference became more pronounced, with air temperatures in the treated area up to 3.5°F lower than in the comparison area. The coating also had a much larger effect on the pavement itself. Surface temperatures fell by as much as about 10°F in the study, showing that the material altered how the ground absorbed and released heat.The results were encouraging, but reflective pavement is not a complete solution to urban heat. A highly reflective surface can send more solar radiation back into the surrounding environment. That can reduce the amount of heat stored in the pavement, but it can also affect the radiant heat experienced by people standing or walking nearby. This distinction matters because air temperature is only one part of how hot a person feels. The temperature of surrounding surfaces, direct sunlight, wind and humidity all influence thermal comfort.Earlier research on cool pavements in Los Angeles examined the issue from a pedestrian perspective. Researchers found that reflective pavement could lower surface temperatures, but its effects on human heat exposure were more complicated because reflected radiation can influence the heat received by people nearby. The findings suggest that reflective pavement should not be treated the same as shading. A tree canopy reduces solar radiation before it reaches people and other surfaces. Reflective pavement changes how the surface responds to sunlight after installation. That does not mean reflective pavement is ineffective; it means its benefits depend on whether you measure air temperature, surface temperature or perceived thermal comfort.The Los Angeles experiment also raises questions about how reflective pavement performs over time. Coatings can weather and lose some of their reflectivity, while roads and other paved surfaces are exposed to traffic, dirt and repeated maintenance.Other research has examined the broader environmental trade-offs of reflective pavement. A life-cycle study of cool-pavement options in Los Angeles and Fresno found that the energy and emissions consequences depend on the materials and construction methods used. Those benefits should be weighed against the impacts of producing and installing the treatment. For Los Angeles, the Pacoima project nevertheless demonstrated that a large area of dark pavement can be altered without completely rebuilding the neighbourhood. During the most extreme heat conditions studied, the treated area was measurably cooler than its nearby comparison area.This experiment does not imply that reflective pavement will by itself be the solution to urban heat issues. Instead, it shows that cities can combine different measures to reduce heat exposure. As global temperatures rise, the question is whether a combination of measures, including reflective pavement, shade and trees, can reduce heat exposure in neighbourhoods during extreme heat events.
Article Summary: Los Angeles coated 700,000 sq ft of dark asphalt with reflective material. During extreme heat, local air was up to 1.9°C cooler. Results suggest that changing the surface of a city can influence the heat experienced around it. But the experiment also highlighted the limits of reflective pavement.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Hulk Hogan: "If I have a problem with someone I talk about them. I don't…" - a lesson on respect, accountability and keeping personal conflicts where they belong
Article Text:
Hulk Hogan

Quote of the day by Hulk Hogan

"If I have a problem with someone I talk about them. I don't pick on their kids"

What is the meaning behind the quote by Hulk Hogan

Why keeping conflict contained actually matters

Why children specifically should never be part of adult disputes

Why saying things directly usually works better than talking around someone

Why taking responsibility for a conflict builds trust

Why respect does not require agreement

Poll Vote & Share your view How do you prefer to handle disagreements? Directly addressing the person involved Avoiding confrontation altogether 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Why this idea reaches well beyond personal disputes

How to actually use this idea

Other famous quotes by Hulk Hogan

"To all my little Hulkamaniacs , say your prayers, take your vitamins and you will never go wrong."

"I'm the man that made wrestling famous."

"The best wrestlers, whether it's a Hulk Hogan or a Rey Mysterio, are the ones who have psychology and can understand this business."

"Whatcha gonna do, when Hulkamania runs wild on you!"

Why this quote still matters today

Disagreements happen to everyone, at work, at home, in public life. What actually separates a fair fight from an unfair one is often not the disagreement itself, but who ends up caught in the middle of it. Hulk Hogan , the professional wrestler, put a simple boundary around exactly that. "If I have a problem with someone I talk about them," he said. "I don't pick on their kids." The quote appears to date from a genuinely difficult stretch of his life, around his very public divorce, when his own family became a regular subject of tabloid coverage. It is a short line, but it holds a genuinely useful boundary that plenty of people forget to draw once a disagreement actually gets heated.The quote lays out two very different ways of handling a conflict. The first is direct and honest. If Hogan has a problem with someone, he talks about it openly with them, rather than letting it fester unspoken. The second draws a firm line. Whatever the disagreement, children stay out of it entirely.The wider point is really about responsibility. A disagreement belongs to the people actually involved in it. Dragging someone else, especially a child who had no part in the dispute, into the middle of it only spreads harm to someone who never asked to be part of the story.Arguments tend to get worse the further they spread beyond the original disagreement. Bringing in friends, relatives or colleagues who had nothing to do with the original issue usually makes things messier and harder to resolve, not easier. Keeping a disagreement focused on the actual people and the actual issue gives it a real chance of being sorted out fairly.Children rely on the adults around them for stability, not for being pulled into arguments they had no hand in creating. Whether the dispute happens inside a family, in public life, or anywhere else, dragging a child into it tends to leave lasting damage on someone who genuinely bears no responsibility for any of it. Hogan's line reflects something most people already agree with instinctively, that children deserve to be protected from conflicts that were never theirs to begin with.Plenty of disagreements get worse simply because people avoid speaking honestly with the person they actually have the issue with. Complaining to everyone except that person, or letting a misunderstanding quietly grow, rarely improves anything. Speaking directly at least gives both sides the chance to explain themselves and possibly find some common ground, even if the disagreement itself never fully disappears.Relationships hold together better when people take real responsibility for their own words and actions. Blaming people who were never actually involved, or letting a dispute spread wider than it needs to, wears trust down quickly. Owning a disagreement honestly, rather than spreading it around, is really a sign of maturity more than anything else. It also tends to make the actual conflict easier to resolve, since energy stays focused on the real issue instead of getting diluted across a wider circle of people who were never part of the original problem.Two people can disagree strongly and still treat each other decently throughout. Respect is not about seeing eye to eye. It is about recognising that everyone involved, and especially anyone not involved at all, deserves fair treatment regardless of how the disagreement itself turns out.Although Hogan is talking specifically about children, the same logic clearly applies more broadly. At work, criticism should stay focused on someone's actual performance rather than turning personal. In public debate, disagreements work best when they stay about the actual ideas rather than drifting toward unrelated people. Families and community groups run into the same pattern too, where an argument between two people quietly expands to involve neighbours, siblings, or friends who never had any stake in the original disagreement at all. The underlying rule stays the same everywhere it applies. Challenge the actual issue. Leave uninvolved people out of it entirely.Take disagreements directly to the person involved rather than letting them spread. Keep family members and colleagues who had nothing to do with it out of the argument entirely. Focus criticism on behaviour, not personal attacks. Protect children specifically from disputes that were never theirs. And remember that a calm, direct conversation usually gets further than an emotional public reaction ever does.Disagreements now spread far faster than they ever used to, thanks to social media, and something that once stayed private can go public within minutes. That makes the basic principle behind Hogan's line more relevant, not less. Having a problem with someone does not give anyone licence to drag people who had nothing to do with it, especially children, into the middle of it. Mature conflict is not really measured by how strongly two people disagree. It is measured by whether they keep that disagreement where it actually belongs, and whether the people around them stay untouched by something that was never theirs to carry.
Article Summary: "If I have a problem with someone I talk about them. I don't pick on their kids" is the quote of the day. What separates a fair fight from an unfair one is often not the disagreement itself, but who ends up caught in it. The quote lays out two very different ways of handling a conflict.

Article Title: Pentagon under fire after revising Iran war casualty count
Article Text:
Photo credit: NYC

The Pentagon has come under scrutiny after reducing the official death toll of US service members killed in the Iran war from 18 to 14 on its website, triggering criticism from military families, veterans and lawmakers over the transparency of its casualty reporting.According to a The New York Times report, the four service members recently killed in Jordan and Iraq were removed from the official tally because they died after President Donald Trump declared a ceasefire, despite the president publicly citing the total number of war dead as 18 days earlier.The acting press secretary for the Pentagon, Joel Valdez, on Thursday attributed the change to “temporary data disruptions” on the website that he suggested would be quickly fixed.The revised casualty count has sparked criticism from military families, veterans and democratic lawmakers, who accused the Pentagon of failing to provide a transparent and timely accounting of the human cost of the conflict.“It is truly disgusting and disheartening to lower the count of our service members who gave their life for this country,” said Tanya Stamos, a Navy veteran and the founder of Operation RJS.She further stated, “As a Navy combat veteran myself, I find it a slap in the face that it is so easy to disregard my brothers and sisters in arms who raised their hand and gave an oath to protect and serve foreign and domestic, all for the government who is choosing to wipe their names from history.”A group of democratic senators has written to defense secretary Pete Hegseth seeking a comprehensive accounting of US personnel killed or wounded during the Iran war, arguing that the American public, Congress and military families are entitled to accurate casualty reporting.After nearly five months of fighting, 18 US service members have been killed in the Iran war. The majority of the fatalities occurred during the conflict's early phase, when Iranian missile and drone attacks targeted American bases across Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Jordan.Nine service members were killed in those attacks, while another six died on March 12 when a US air force KC-135 aerial refuelling aircraft crashed in western Iraq during operational missions.A US navy sailor later died after a helicopter made an emergency landing in the Arabian Sea on July 1, taking the official death toll to 14 before the latest escalation.The remaining four deaths occurred after fighting resumed following the collapse of the ceasefire. On July 18, Iranian ballistic missiles struck Muwaffaq Salti air base in Jordan, killing 3 US service members. A day later, another US service member was killed at Erbil air base in Iraq during the controlled detonation of unexploded ordnance from a downed Iranian drone.
Article Summary: Pentagon has reduced the official death toll of US service members killed in the Iran war from 18 to 14. Four service members recently killed in Jordan and Iraq were removed from the official tally because they died after President Donald Trump declared a ceasefire. The acting press secretary for the Pentagon, Joel Valdez, on Thursday attributed the change to “temporary data disruptions” on the website.

Article Title: PoK heads to polls amid weeks of deadly clashes and political unrest - what to expect
Article Text:
Jaac protests, crackdown and rights concerns cast shadow

Political battle intensifies

Elections to the so-called legislative assembly in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) begin on Monday amid heightened security and continuing political unrest. The three-phase polls come after weeks of violent clashes that have left several people dead and hundreds injured.Polling for the 45 directly elected seats of the 53-member assembly will be conducted in three phases, ending on August 10. The first phase covers 13 constituencies in Mirpur division on Monday. This will be followed by polling in nine constituencies of Muzaffarabad division and all 12 refugee constituencies on August 2, with the remaining 11 constituencies of Poonch division voting on August 10.Ahead of the polls, Pakistan's Punjab province deployed 14,000 police personnel to PoK for election security."The Punjab government has sent 14,000 personnel of Punjab policemen for Kashmir poll security duty on the request of the Kashmir government," a Pakistani government official told news agency PTI."Of these, 30 per cent are carrying weapons and 70 per cent are equipped with anti-riot equipment," the official added.The election schedule was announced by PoK election commissioner Ghulam Mustafa Mughal earlier this month.The assembly comprises 53 seats, of which 45 are directly elected, while eight are reserved for women, technocrats and clerics. Of the total seats, 12 are reserved for refugees who settled in PoK after 1947. Meanwhile, elections to the Gilgit-Baltistan Assembly were held on June 7.The polls are taking place against the backdrop of sustained unrest in the region. The Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) led protests for nearly two months, demanding, among other issues, the abolition of the 12 refugee seats.The demonstrations escalated into violent clashes with security forces, with Pakistani authorities reporting casualties among both protesters and security personnel.Following the unrest, the regional government banned Jaac under anti-terrorism legislation and authorities arrested more than 100 people before and after the clashes, according to PTI.The human rights commission of Pakistan (HRCP) said it was "deeply alarmed" by the violence in PoK, where 11 people, including four police officers, were killed and hundreds injured during clashes. The unrest has also drawn international attention, with the office of the united nations high commissioner for Human Rights expressing concern over the "wave of unrest". UN high commissioner for human rights Volker Türk appealed for calm and said "dozens of people, mostly protesters but also law enforcement personnel, have reportedly been killed since June. "India has reiterated its long-standing position on the region. On July 14, the ministry of external affairs described the protests in PoK as a "direct consequence" of Islamabad's decades-long "systemic exploitation and administrative oppression" in areas under its "forcible" occupation. New Delhi also criticised reported police brutality against protesters.India has consistently maintained that the entire Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, including the areas under Pakistan's control, are "integral and inalienable parts of India" and that Pakistan remains in "illegal and forcible occupation" of parts of these Union Territories.Meanwhile, defence minister Rajnath Singh on Sunday reinforced India's position during his address at the Kargil War Memorial, saying there would be "no talks with Pakistan". "If there will be talks, it will be on Pakistan-Occupied-Kashmir (PoK), a part of India which it occupied illegally," he said. Singh also accused Pakistan of making terrorism "a part of its state policy" and said Operation Sindoor had shown India could respond to any misadventure with a severity "beyond their imagination. "The election is also unfolding alongside political contestation in Pakistan. The Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz is facing its coalition partner, the Pakistan People's Party, in the PoK polls, while former prime minister Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf has boycotted the election.Separately, Pakistan's Punjab government has denied permission to Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf to hold a rally in Lahore on August 5 to mark the third anniversary of Imran Khan's imprisonment. The party has said it will move the court seeking permission for the event.Former prime minister Nawaz Sharif has also expressed his desire to become the prime minister of PoK, saying it would allow him to "personally oversee" the development of the region.
Article Summary: Polling for the 45 directly elected seats of the 53-member assembly will be conducted in three phases, ending on August 10. The assembly comprises 53 seats, of which 45 are directly elected, while eight are reserved for women, technocrats and clerics. Pakistan's Punjab province deployed 14,000 police personnel to PoK for election security.

Article Title: Saudi money, Chinese weapons, American patronage: Can Pakistan balance all three?
Article Text:
Saudi Arabia Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud (MBS), Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir Ahmed Shah, US President Donald Trump, President Xi Jinping.

Growing security cooperation with Saudi Arabia





Balancing act comes with growing risks





Domestic troubles threaten Pakistan's global ambitions





Munir's 'hard state' vision





Economic fragility limits strategic ambitions





NEW DELHI: Pakistan is attempting one of its most ambitious foreign policy balancing acts in decades, seeking to simultaneously preserve its strategic partnership with China, deepen security ties with Saudi Arabia, rebuild relations with US President Donald Trump 's administration, mediate between Washington and Tehran, and strengthen coordination with Turkey and Egypt, according to a detailed Financial Times report.The report says Pakistan's military leadership under Field Marshal Asim Munir believes the country's geopolitical location and longstanding relationships across competing power centres have created a rare opportunity to elevate Islamabad's diplomatic profile despite mounting economic and security challenges at home.According to the report, Pakistan's efforts have become particularly visible during the recent Middle East crisis, with Islamabad attempting to position itself as a regional mediator while simultaneously expanding defence cooperation with Gulf monarchies and maintaining its decades-old strategic partnership with Beijing.However, analysts quoted by the newspaper warn that Pakistan's expanding diplomatic ambitions are unfolding against the backdrop of a fragile economy, worsening militancy and growing political repression, raising questions about whether Islamabad can sustain such an ambitious foreign policy.According to the report, Pakistan today finds itself pursuing an unusually complex foreign policy that requires it to balance sometimes competing strategic relationships.The newspaper says Islamabad is simultaneously:Former Pakistani brigadier Feroz Khan, quoted by the FT, says Pakistan has increasingly relied on diplomacy and military influence to compensate for its domestic weaknesses."Given its deep economic and political weaknesses, [Pakistan's] nuclear bomb, its conventional military forces and diplomacy are all it has to punch above its weight as a middle power," says Khan, who now teaches at the Naval Postgraduate School in California.According to the newspaper, Pakistan's military establishment believes the Middle East offers Islamabad greater strategic space than South Asia, where India's economic and military strength limits Pakistan's regional influence."As a south Asian power, Pakistan is permanently number two to India, the wealthier, stronger and more useful nation to the US in that region," Khan says. "But in the Middle East, it believes it can come into its own, with the blessing of US Central Command and Saudi Arabia."The report says Islamabad's diplomatic outreach has coincided with efforts by Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Turkey to play larger roles in shaping the region's post-war security architecture.According to analysts cited by the newspaper, this emerging grouping could eventually serve as a counterweight to growing military cooperation involving the United Arab Emirates, Israel and India.According to FT, one of the clearest illustrations of Pakistan's growing role came shortly before Islamabad hosted talks involving the United States and Iran earlier this year.The newspaper reports that on April 10, Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed al-Jadaan visited Islamabad and met Pakistan's military chief Field Marshal Asim Munir at the Prime Minister House.Citing two people briefed on the discussions, FT says Saudi Arabia requested Pakistan's military support as the kingdom came under missile and drone attacks allegedly launched by Iran.According to the report, Riyadh had already signed a mutual defence agreement with Islamabad in 2025 and wanted Pakistan to provide personnel and military equipment.The newspaper says Pakistan's leadership was initially reluctant because such a move could complicate its planned mediation efforts between Washington and Tehran and trigger domestic political criticism from sections of Pakistan's population sympathetic to Iran.However, according to the report, Pakistan was also under severe financial pressure.The report says that only days earlier, the United Arab Emirates had unexpectedly demanded repayment of $3.5 billion in loans, equivalent to roughly one-fifth of Pakistan's foreign exchange reserves at the time.According to the newspaper, Pakistan eventually agreed to Saudi Arabia's request.The FT, citing people familiar with the matter, reports that Munir dispatched a squadron of fighter aircraft, air force personnel and a Chinese-made HQ-9 air defence system to a Saudi military base overlooking Iran's coastline.The report further claims that Saudi Arabia extended a $3 billion loan to Pakistan the following week.Pakistan's military spokesperson Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry rejected any suggestion that the deployment and the loan were linked."This is a special, decades-old relationship based on a very strong religious foundation and mutual respect," Chaudhry told the FT.The Saudi episode reflects a broader effort by Field Marshal Asim Munir to reshape Pakistan's international standing.According to the newspaper, Munir has sought to leverage Pakistan's longstanding relationships with China, Saudi Arabia and the United States while simultaneously presenting Islamabad as a credible diplomatic intermediary in regional crises.The report says Munir hopes to transform Pakistan into what he calls a "hard state" capable of restoring internal stability, defeating militancy, attracting foreign investment and projecting greater influence abroad.One former US diplomat who dealt extensively with Munir told the FT that the army chief "rules Pakistan with a 'massive chip on his shoulder'" and is determined to strengthen the country's security apparatus."Munir aspires to turn Pakistan into what he calls a 'hard state' and rules Pakistan with a 'massive chip on his shoulder'," the former diplomat said.According to the newspaper, Munir has increasingly concentrated power within Pakistan's military establishment since becoming army chief in November 2022.The Pakistan's parliament has granted him expanded authority, including extending his tenure and giving him greater oversight over the armed forces while critics accuse the government of weakening judicial independence and restricting political dissent.Analysts quoted by the newspaper argue that Munir believes tighter military control is necessary to restore order after years of political instability and economic decline.Yet, according to the report, Pakistan's growing diplomatic activism abroad contrasts sharply with the challenges confronting the country at home, including rising militant violence, slowing investment, mounting debt and increasing dependence on external financial assistance.According to the FT, Pakistan's current foreign policy rests on maintaining close ties with three major powers whose interests often diverge: China, Saudi Arabia and the United States.The newspaper says Beijing remains Islamabad's largest defence supplier and one of its most important strategic partners, while Saudi Arabia has become Pakistan's principal financial backer. At the same time, Pakistan has worked to rebuild ties with Washington under US President Donald Trump, despite decades of fluctuating relations.Pakistan military spokesperson Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry told the Financial Times that Islamabad's relationships with Beijing and Riyadh differ from conventional diplomatic partnerships."There are two countries with whom Pakistan has a special relationship: China and Saudi Arabia," Chaudhry said. "With them, there is never a quid pro quo."According to FT report, China has invested more than $30 billion in Pakistan through infrastructure, transport and power projects, including development of the strategically important Gwadar Port under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). Beijing has also played a central role in Pakistan's nuclear, missile and defence programmes over several decades and continues to be its largest supplier of military equipment.Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, remains Pakistan's biggest financial lifeline, according to the report. Besides repeated loans and deferred payment facilities, Riyadh has frequently rolled over debt repayments to help Islamabad avoid a balance-of-payments crisis.The Pakistan currently owes Saudi Arabia around $8 billion, equivalent to nearly 46 per cent of the country's central bank reserves, making the Gulf kingdom one of Islamabad's most important creditors.The FT report says Pakistan has also sought to restore relations with the United States after years of strained ties.According to the newspaper, Islamabad nominated Donald Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize in June last year for what it described as his "decisive diplomatic intervention" during Pakistan's brief military conflict with India.The report notes that Trump, who had once accused Pakistan of giving the United States "nothing but lies and deceit", has since publicly referred to Asim Munir as his "favourite field marshal", reflecting what the newspaper describes as one of the warmest periods in US-Pakistan relations in recent years.Accroding to the report, Washington also gave Pakistan greater diplomatic space during the recent Middle East crisis.Asfandyar Mir, senior fellow for South Asia at the Stimson Center in Washington, told the newspaper Munir had taken a considerable political gamble by placing Pakistan at the centre of diplomatic efforts."Munir took a significant risk by staking his standing on diplomacy that could easily have backfired," Mir said."But Trump, in a departure from the India-centric consensus that has defined American policy for a decade, allowed Pakistan to make its play."According to the report, Pakistan viewed improved ties with Washington as essential not only for regional diplomacy but also for maintaining access to Western financial institutions at a time when the country's economy remains heavily dependent on IMF support.According to the Financial Times, Pakistan attempted to use its relationships with both Iran and the United States to position itself as a neutral intermediary during the recent conflict.The newspaper reports that Asim Munir chaired marathon discussions between US Vice President JD Vance and Iranian representatives that eventually laid the groundwork for what the report describes as the "Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding", a 14-point ceasefire agreement.However, according to the Financial Times, those diplomatic gains proved short-lived after President Trump later declared the ceasefire "over" following renewed Iranian attacks on commercial shipping and authorised fresh military strikes.The newspaper says Tehran responded with missile and drone attacks against Gulf states while once again disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route through which most of Pakistan's imported oil passes.Despite the renewed conflict, Pakistan's military insists Islamabad continues to pursue diplomacy."Pakistan has a clear interest in peace in the larger Muslim world, and particularly the Gulf," Chaudhry told the Financial Times. "The countries of the Gulf know this and are therefore more comfortable dealing with us as a security partner and honest broker."The military spokesperson also said Pakistan had remained engaged with all major regional stakeholders."Pakistan has been working with all of the stakeholders in the Gulf as well as Iran to ensure that this war should not spiral and should not expand," Chaudhry said.The Financial Times says Pakistan's mediation efforts have coincided with rapidly expanding military cooperation with Saudi Arabia.According to the report, the two countries signed a mutual defence agreement in September 2025 that has not been made public but was approved without parliamentary debate.The newspaper says official statements from both governments described the agreement as stating that "any aggression against either country shall be considered an aggression against both."According to a person briefed on the discussions, cited by the Financial Times, Islamabad and Riyadh are also exploring the creation of a joint aerial defence system following vulnerabilities exposed during attacks on Saudi infrastructure.The newspaper says closer defence cooperation also serves Pakistan's own economic interests.More than 5.5 million Pakistanis work across Gulf countries, sending home over $20 billion annually in remittances that remain one of Pakistan's largest sources of foreign exchange.Umer Karim of the Riyadh-based King Faisal Centre for Research and Islamic Studies told the Financial Times that Saudi Arabia has repeatedly acted as Pakistan's financial backstop."In Saudi Arabia, you have a state which will always at least try to provide you with a degree of financial cushion in moments of great need," Karim said.The Financial Times says Pakistan's increasingly close relationship with Saudi Arabia also exposes Islamabad to new strategic vulnerabilities.According to the report, Pakistan remains heavily dependent on Saudi financial assistance while also sharing deep religious, cultural and historical ties with neighbouring Iran.The newspaper notes that Pakistan is home to one of the world's largest Shia populations, estimated at around 40 million, making any perceived tilt towards Riyadh politically sensitive.According to the Financial Times, tensions became particularly evident after the assassination of Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei earlier this year, which reportedly triggered riots in several Pakistani cities that left at least two dozen people dead.The report also says Pakistan faced additional financial pressure when the United Arab Emirates demanded immediate repayment of $3.5 billion in loans, reflecting what analysts describe as growing geopolitical competition within the Gulf.Karim warned that Pakistan's dependence on Saudi Arabia could eventually leave it with limited diplomatic flexibility."Considering Pakistan's indispensable financial dependence on Saudi Arabia, it essentially won't have much of a choice," he told the Financial Times.The newspaper concludes that Pakistan's attempt to simultaneously retain Chinese strategic support, Saudi financial backing and improved relations with Washington economy continues to struggle under mounting debt, repeated balance-of-payments crises and dependence on international lenders.
